title: Gabriel Byrne Walking With Ghosts - review with pictures
transcript: hello welcome to one minute theater reviews i'm paul several lewis and i'm here at the apollo theater in london to see gabriel byrne walking with ghosts i realized that those ghosts were not really walking with me they were inside me walking with ghosts is an autobiographical play from an actor who has appeared in around 70 films including the usual suspects and miller's crossing but if you're expecting hollywood gossip you're going to be deeply disappointed the ghosts that gabriel byrne talks about are mainly from his childhood and youth he conjures up the people from his past with the power of language and his prowess as an actor the lights go up and mr burn reminiscent of the ancient mariner immediately holds you with his glittering eye and launches into his monologue i had a dream he says and tells us of the ghost boy always running that is him as a child what follows are more than anecdotes of a guest on a chat show they're an exploration of memory the way some images linger while others fade the events trivial and momentous that made an impression and made the man that we now see before us his stories are funny sad sentimental shocking but always captivating even if they are about an ordinary vulnerable frightened man rather than an extraordinary actor if i have a reservation it's that we are never so drawn into his tales that we forget he is an actor seducing us with his art well that's a one minute review but keep watching for more on gabriel byrne walking with ghosts he's dressed in a way we might call smart casual uh but not cheap designed by jonah cleary his outfit comprises tones of blue from a blue jacket and trousers to a cornflower blue shirt and sapphire blue leather shoes his hair may be a little wild which i guess is a kind of trademark of his but he looks fit and a lot younger than 72 well he must be fit to be alone on stage and hold the audience's attention for nearly two hours he was born and brought up in ireland of course and there's a certain familiarity in his tales of an irish catholic childhood similar characters and even experiences crop up in many irish people's reminiscences mr burns talent is to bring them to life with a just with a gesture or a look so that he inhabits the characters he's describing like springsprom who worked in the library who walked on the pavement as if it was a mattress how's it going lads [Music] and he also employs the language of a poet the beautiful image or the unexpected metaphor as when he talks of a woman's teeth being like a row of refrigerators it was a poor childhood there's a touching scene where he imitates his mother counting out coins to pay for his outfit but despite a lack of open affection from his parents something which many people of my generation will be familiar with certain unexpected incidents made it clear to him that he was loved for someone reputed to be a private person gabriel byrne shares or appears to be sharing extremely personal stories from his life um there appears to be almost an element of catharsis when he talks about being sexually abused as a child the unforeseen heartbreaking tragedy that affected his sister his own alcoholism which is almost foretold in one of the earliest scenes when the famous potent player brendan beahan drunkenly blesses him as a small child on a bus it may not be a hollywood gossip story but it is an actor's story and we see and share his love of acting the magic of his first visit to the cinema something that along with eating a bowl of cornflakes was not allowed by his mother but indulged by his grandmother we feel in his face the ghost boy's reaction to the action on the big screen the excitement the fear the laughter the tears the lovely dark womb of the cinema as he calls it ignites a love that is never extinguished through subsequent and often humorous attempts at careers as a priest a teacher a plumber a washer upper and more then as the second app begins he joins an am dram company at last i felt that i belonged and we see him learning the craft from a seasoned actor his demonstration of how to do a double take is hilarious as are his descriptions of the various kinds of bow that actors do during their curtain court we do get a glimpse of one hollywood icon richard burton who tells him that fame doesn't change you but it changes the people who meet you they get drunk together leading mr burns to describe vividly the attraction of drink the self-deception of addiction and his momentous but successful struggle to break free of his alcoholism he doesn't linger on his movie career but returns to talk about his family because as i said this is not about stripping away the phony tinsel of hollywood to find the real tinsel underneath as someone once said this is a personal story well supported by his director lonnie price who keeps him moving around the stage and a set by sinead mckenna comprising a stool a bench and a desk and chair and then a picture frame within a picture frame within a frame as if taking us back in time and at the back a cracked mirror suggesting the unreliability of memory sounds by sinead diskin help invoke the situations being described and as we're near the end of the play mr burns description of the vicissitudes of growing old will not be surprising to anyone who's had elderly parents but he brings his own aging and dying parents to life in a heart-tugging manner mr burns ability to switch in a moment from one character to another and summon them to life with a gesture or an expression add up to a master class in both acting and storytelling which are perhaps the same thing but seeing him up close performing for two hours you do begin to see too well how it's done the slight stuttering the repeating of the repeating of and so on i found that the artifice that enables him to tell the story also acted as a barrier to my becoming fully involved nevertheless i thoroughly recommend seeing this great actor at work evoking the ghosts of his past and i give gabriel burns walking with ghosts four stars being useful if you did why not subscribe to
